title: Lessons from Slush 2025: How Harvey Is Scaling Domain-Specific AI for Legal and Beyond
author: ComplexDiscovery Staff

dom.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core thesis that durable legal-AI value lies in specialist infrastructure and lawyer-informed workflows rather than foundation models alone. It materially extends that thesis by describing Harvey’s evolution from an individual-lawyer copilot into a firm-level platform aimed at matter management, workflow optimisation, client collaboration and profitability, although it supplies no outcome data proving those gains.
qs: “We think of a lot of the product as not going to be the models, it’s going to be all of the infrastructure around them,” Pereyra noted.

“As we’ve scaled, really the value prop that we want to sell to law firms is we will make your business better.”  This shift means focusing on platform capabilities that improve firm profitability through better client matter management, workflow optimization, and direct collaboration between law firms and their clients on Harvey’s platform.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that AI will augment rather than replace lawyers and that reliable delivery requires human verification. It materially extends the proposition through Harvey’s concrete strategy of using major law firms as design partners and converting firms’ and clients’ proprietary expertise and data into AI systems, reinforcing the importance of institutional knowledge and controlled implementation.
qs: Pereyra emphasized that the first 10, 20, and 50 hires “really set the foundation of the culture of the company,” focusing on finding people who “cared as much as Winston and I did.”  Quality assurance remains paramount, with human-in-the-loop systems ensuring accuracy.

Rather than replacing lawyers, Pereyra sees AI giving knowledge workers “so much more leverage,” predicting that “the top most skilled knowledge workers will actually be more successful than they are today.”  Looking ahead, Harvey is exploring how to help law firms and clients convert their expertise and private data into AI systems.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s emphasis on domain expertise, human oversight, risk management and workflow integration rather than technical capability alone. It materially extends the proposition by framing AI as embedded professional infrastructure that can encode private institutional knowledge into domain-specific systems and support longer-duration, end-to-end workflows, though these are presented chiefly as strategy and prediction rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: By embedding domain expertise directly into AI workflows and focusing on seamless integration with existing professional practices, Harvey has shown that specificity is essential.

For eDiscovery platforms, governance software vendors, and cybersecurity service providers, Harvey’s emphasis on human oversight, data security, and clear adoption pathways provides a blueprint for building AI products that are both powerful and trustworthy.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core thesis that Harvey is evolving from an individual copilot into domain-specific infrastructure for legal workflows. It treats embedded legal expertise, firm–client collaboration, human oversight and trust as central to adoption, while presenting growth and end-to-end agentic capabilities as promising but not independently validated evidence of quality, profitability or workforce effects.

It also endorses human oversight and trust-centred adoption, without supplying independent accuracy or productivity evidence; its workforce and monetisation claims remain prospective.

It also aligns with differentiation through encoded institutional knowledge and governance, although it offers strategic claims rather than measured returns and does not substantively address bargaining shifts, ALSPs or pricing change.

st.an: The source supports the proposition that organisational value depends on firm-wide infrastructure, workflow optimisation, domain-specific implementation and human oversight rather than access to an individual copilot or model capability alone. Its growth and profitability claims remain strategic or anecdotal rather than measured evidence of realised value.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s application-layer thesis by locating value in legal expertise, workflow integration, human oversight and infrastructure around foundation models. Its growth metrics show demand, while its profitability, employment and legal-system benefits remain ambitions rather than proof of performance or durable defensibility.

kp.k: Harvey reports rapid international legal AI expansion
kp.d: ComplexDiscovery’s November 19, 2025 report on Gabe Pereyra’s Slush presentation describes Harvey as a legal and professional-services AI platform serving over 700 customers across 58 countries in three years, generating more than $100 million in annual recurring revenue and employing over 500 people. These are reported company growth figures, rather than findings from a study of legal-sector adoption. Early demonstrations to Allen & Overy and PwC UK made international customers central from the outset.
qs: Harvey, an AI platform built specifically for legal and professional services, has grown to serve over 700 customers across 58 countries in just three years, generating more than $100 million in annual recurring revenue.
OpenAI provided seed funding, and the team’s first major demonstration went to Allen & Overy in the UK, followed by PwC UK — making Harvey an international company from the start.

kp.k: Early associate-task experiments suggested potential for agents
kp.d: Pereyra recounts co-founder Winston Weinberg spending 14 hours testing early language models and reporting that he had accomplished associate-level legal work. Pereyra linked this experience with his reinforcement-learning research to the prospect of building agents. The account is a founder-origin anecdote, not a measured assessment of task performance or lawyer replacement.
qs: The breakthrough moment came when Weinberg spent 14 hours testing early models.
“I did all of it,” Weinberg told Pereyra after his marathon session, referring to the associate-level legal work he had accomplished using the models.
“When I saw that combined with the research I’d done at DeepMind in reinforcement learning, it was so clear you would be able to build these agents,” Pereyra recalled.

kp.k: Language alignment and embedded lawyers supported adoption
kp.d: Pereyra attributes unexpectedly rapid law-firm adoption to AI’s fit with language-intensive legal work, contrasting it with earlier technologies. He also credits lawyers embedded in product and sales teams with shaping product development and communicating value. The article presents domain expertise and trust as explanations for Harvey’s adoption.
qs: “I think historically lawyers haven’t been tech-forward because the tech has not been based around language, and so much of the work they do is language-based,” he explained.
“But I think it was actually surprising to most people how quickly these law firms adopted this technology.”

“We got a bunch of lawyers early on the sales side,” Pereyra said, noting that having “lawyers from big law” on both the product and sales teams “really shaped how we thought about both building the product and communicating the value.”

kp.k: Strategy shifts from individual copilot to firm infrastructure
kp.d: Pereyra describes a shift from augmenting individual lawyers to improving law-firm businesses. The article identifies matter management, workflow optimization and direct firm-client collaboration as intended routes to profitability. Infrastructure surrounding models becomes a principal product focus; these statements describe strategic aims rather than quantified profitability gains.
qs: “When we first built the product, it was a co-pilot for individual lawyers,” Pereyra explained.
“As we’ve scaled, really the value prop that we want to sell to law firms is we will make your business better.”

This shift means focusing on platform capabilities that improve firm profitability through better client matter management, workflow optimization, and direct collaboration between law firms and their clients on Harvey’s platform.
“We think of a lot of the product as not going to be the models, it’s going to be all of the infrastructure around them,” Pereyra noted.

kp.k: Human oversight and law-firm partnerships underpin quality assurance
kp.d: The article characterizes human-in-the-loop systems as central to accuracy. Pereyra says large law firms were chosen as design partners because of their error-prevention practices and that Harvey learned from those partnerships. No measured accuracy or error rates accompany this account of quality assurance.
qs: Quality assurance remains paramount, with human-in-the-loop systems ensuring accuracy.

“Part of why we wanted to start working with the largest law firms is they are one of the best industries in the world at making sure that you don’t make mistakes,” Pereyra said, noting that Harvey has “learned a ton in working with them as design partners.”

kp.k: European expansion combines privacy challenges and multilingual partnerships
kp.d: The report identifies 70 London employees and partnerships with EQT, Mistral and Eleven Labs as elements of Harvey’s European presence. Pereyra highlights unresolved regulatory and data-privacy problems and describes multilingual, dialect-sensitive voice functionality as a goal, alongside emerging government access-to-justice work.
qs: With Europe as Harvey’s initial market, the company maintains a strong presence there with 70 employees in its London office.
Recent strategic partnerships include collaborations with EQT, open-source model provider Mistral, and voice AI company Eleven Labs to expand multilingual capabilities.
“There’s a lot of interesting regulatory data privacy problems that we want to solve,” Pereyra said about European expansion.

The Eleven Labs partnership will help “make Harvey’s voice work in every language and all of the different regions with the right dialect,” as Harvey begins working with government systems on access to justice initiatives.

kp.k: Pereyra predicts augmentation rather than lawyer replacement
kp.d: Against concerns about junior-lawyer displacement, Pereyra expresses optimism about entering high-skilled knowledge professions and predicts greater success for the most skilled workers. This is a forward-looking view supported by an analogy to his experience learning programming, not employment evidence or a specified forecast horizon. His quoted use of leverage concerns worker capability, not a stated associate-to-partner staffing ratio.
qs: “I don’t think there’s a better time than now to enter these very high-skilled knowledge work professions,” he said, comparing the current moment to his own experience learning programming a decade ago.

Rather than replacing lawyers, Pereyra sees AI giving knowledge workers “so much more leverage,” predicting that “the top most skilled knowledge workers will actually be more successful than they are today.”

kp.k: Private professional expertise becomes a potential monetizable AI asset
kp.d: Pereyra describes exploratory work to help law firms, professional-service providers and clients convert private knowledge and expertise into AI systems and models with new monetization opportunities. The article presents this as a developing capability, without specifying commercial arrangements or realized revenues.
qs: “Law firms and professional service providers have some of the most unique human knowledge in the world, but it’s all private,” Pereyra explained.
The company is developing ways to help organizations “convert that relationship, that expertise into AI systems, into models and monetize those in new ways.”

kp.k: Access-to-justice ambitions extend to legal-system design
kp.d: Pereyra distinguishes providing individuals with high-quality legal services from the broader ambition of helping societies design better legal systems. He reports some work with court systems in various countries, but does not identify jurisdictions, interventions or outcomes. These ambitions extend beyond enterprise efficiency to public-facing legal services and institutional reform.
qs: Pereyra described two levels of access to justice: providing high-quality legal services to individuals, and the “even more exciting” possibility of helping societies “figure out better legal systems.”
“We’ve done some things with court systems in various countries,” Pereyra revealed.

kp.k: Professional workflows could become reinforcement-learning environments
kp.d: Pereyra identifies turning products into reinforcement-learning environments as a future direction. The article describes systems learning from long-term, end-to-end professional tasks while retaining the rigor required in regulated industries; it does not report demonstrated results from this approach.
qs: As Pereyra noted about the future of AI in professional services, the focus is shifting to “figuring out how to turn your product into these reinforcement learning environments,” where systems can learn from long-term, end-to-end professional tasks while maintaining the rigor required in highly regulated industries.

kp.k: Article generalizes trust-first lessons to adjacent regulated sectors
kp.d: ComplexDiscovery argues that cybersecurity, information-governance and eDiscovery providers can learn from Harvey’s domain-specific approach. Its recommendations emphasize integration with existing professional practices, human oversight, data security, adoption pathways and long-term risk management. This is the publication’s cross-domain interpretation of Harvey’s trajectory, rather than comparative evidence establishing the same outcomes elsewhere.
qs: The company’s success demonstrates that trust, rather than technical sophistication alone, drives adoption in regulated environments.

For eDiscovery platforms, governance software vendors, and cybersecurity service providers, Harvey’s emphasis on human oversight, data security, and clear adoption pathways provides a blueprint for building AI products that are both powerful and trustworthy.
Success requires not just cutting-edge models but thoughtful product decisions that prioritize risk management and long-term trust.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Pereyra attributes rapid legal-AI adoption to the fit between language models and lawyers’ language-based work, supported by embedded legal expertise.
pts.d: Pereyra says law firms adopted the technology surprisingly quickly despite their reputation for technological conservatism. He attributes Harvey’s product development and communication of value partly to recruiting lawyers into product and sales. ComplexDiscovery reports that Harvey reached over 700 customers in 58 countries and more than $100 million in annual recurring revenue within three years. These are reported company-scale indicators, rather than measurements of legal-work outcomes.

pts.k: Pereyra describes a shift from individual-lawyer assistance toward firm-wide business improvement through AI infrastructure.
pts.d: Harvey’s initial model was a copilot for individual lawyers. Pereyra now frames its intended value as improving the law firm’s business. ComplexDiscovery describes the mechanisms as better client matter management, workflow optimization and direct firm–client collaboration, intended to improve profitability. This is a strategic value proposition, not a reported quantified profitability result. Pereyra also anticipates professional-task learning environments built around products rather than models alone.

pts.k: Pereyra predicts augmentation rather than lawyer replacement, with particularly strong benefits for the most skilled knowledge workers.
pts.d: Responding to concerns about junior-lawyer displacement, Pereyra expresses optimism about entering high-skilled professions and predicts greater success for top-skilled workers. His reference to greater 'leverage' means amplified individual capability in this passage, not an associate-to-partner staffing ratio. The article does not specify employment levels, junior hiring effects or a staffing structure resulting from this prediction.

pts.k: Pereyra anticipates new monetization of firms’ private expertise and client relationships through AI systems.
pts.d: Harvey is exploring and developing ways for law firms, professional service providers and their clients to turn proprietary knowledge and private data into AI systems or models. Pereyra presents this as a potential new revenue mechanism; the article supplies no implemented example, revenue estimate or specified commercial model.

pts.k: Pereyra presents AI as a potential means of expanding individual access to legal services and improving legal systems.
pts.d: The article distinguishes an ambition to provide high-quality legal services to individuals from a broader ambition to help societies improve legal systems. Pereyra reports some work with court systems, while the article says Harvey is beginning government access-to-justice initiatives. Multilingual voice capabilities are a planned enabling feature. No countries, service volumes, affordability effects or access-to-justice outcomes are specified.

pts.k: ComplexDiscovery generalizes Harvey’s experience into a trust- and infrastructure-led model for AI adoption in regulated professional services.
pts.d: The staff authors claim that trust, domain expertise, human oversight, security and integration with existing work practices drive adoption and create collaborative systems that improve decision-making. They extend this lesson to eDiscovery, information governance and cybersecurity providers. This is the authors’ cross-domain interpretation of Harvey’s trajectory, rather than a separately demonstrated result in those markets.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies on founder testimony, an early-use anecdote, reported commercial growth and named business relationships.
pts.d: The article reports Pereyra’s November 19, 2025 Slush discussion. Its evidence includes his account of Weinberg spending 14 hours testing early models on associate-level work, early demonstrations to Allen & Overy and PwC UK, lawyers embedded in Harvey’s teams, large-law-firm design partnerships, and collaborations with EQT, Mistral and Eleven Labs. The early task-completion account is an anecdote relayed by Pereyra, not an independently assessed test. Reported customer, revenue and staffing figures illustrate commercial expansion. No task benchmark, measured accuracy rate, controlled productivity study, quantified client savings or labor-market evidence is supplied. The publication’s percentage-based content assessment rates the article itself, not AI performance.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current adoption and quality-control claims are anchored to November 2025; broader transformation, monetization and justice ambitions have no fixed delivery dates.
pts.d: The growth figures cover approximately the three years preceding the November 19, 2025 article. The copilot-to-platform shift is described as underway. Private-knowledge monetization is exploratory or in development; government and court work is early and unspecified; universal multilingual voice is an intended partnership outcome. Workforce optimism concerns entrants now and future success without a forecast horizon. The source conditions successful regulated-industry deployment on human-in-the-loop checking, domain expertise, integration, data security, privacy and rigorous quality controls. Human oversight here is verification of outputs, not evidence from benchmarking, and the source does not establish an autonomous replacement model.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed changes span individual lawyers, law-firm businesses and clients, professional-service providers, and public legal institutions.
pts.d: Individual lawyers are offered assistance and increased capability; the most skilled knowledge workers are predicted to gain especially, while junior displacement concerns receive an optimistic response rather than a quantified forecast. Large law firms feature as early adopters and design partners. Firms and their clients are prospective beneficiaries of improved workflows, shared collaboration and monetized proprietary expertise. Individuals needing legal help, governments and courts are the intended beneficiaries of justice initiatives. eDiscovery platforms, governance vendors and cybersecurity service providers are invited to apply the authors’ adoption lessons. Harvey is the software-platform vendor in this account, not an ALSP delivering legal work.
